teachings.summary: After all is vanity, the conclusion is to fear God and keep His commandments, for every work will come into judgment and abundant life is in serving Him.
teachings.text:
All wisdom comes from the Lord. Jesus is that good shepherd. His words are as goads to cattle, the sharp and pronged sticks used to guide the herd. As nails of a master builder, sure and true. Holding the whole house together. Built upon the rock, which Jesus likes His sayings.

The word of God is sufficient to admonish, to guide and be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works.

We may write and study an infinite number of books by men, the ways of this world. But the only way we need is God's. Studying to be approved by Him.

*Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man.*

Having considered all these things and having observed all he could, knowing there is nothing new under the Sun, and that what is discovered today was known before and will be forgotten and known again in the future, Solomon the Wise comes to the ultimate conclusion that the purpose of life isn't gathering riches, or pleasure or mirth. It is not toil and working endlessly, only to be forgotten. It is only to fear God and keep His commandments. This is the whole duty of man.

**Hebrews 9:27**
*And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment*

**Luke 8:17**
*For nothing is secret, that shall not be made manifest; neither any thing hid, that shall not be known and come abroad.*

We all have an appointment with death. And a time of judgment before the Lord*, Who will render to every man according to his deeds*.

*For God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether it be good, or whether it be evil.*

Vanity, vanity, all is vanity. But faith in the Lord, fearing Him only and keeping His ways and wisdom, in all our ways acknowledging Him that He may direct our paths...this is the secret to life.

As Jesus says in **John 10:10** *...I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.*

With this, the sermon ends. The matter is settled. Life is a gift from God, and an abundant life is in service of Him. The true meaning of it all is to give Him glory. Our purpose is to be known of Him that we may know Christ.

Amen

teachings.title: How the fool, wise and righteous learn
teachings.summary: The fool never learns, the wise learn from others, the righteous learn from God's word, while the wicked and hypocrites know right and abuse it.
teachings.text:
The fool never learns right from wrong from experience. They do the same foolishness over and over again and expect it to work out differently "this time."

The average person learns right and wrong from their own experience, imperfectly.

The wise learn what's right and wrong not only from their own, but by others'experiences.

The righteous learns what's right and wrong from God's word, and believe Him when He says something is so.

The wicked know what is right from wrong and do it anyway. Knowing the judgment of God, yet they don't care.

The hypocrite knows what's right from wrong and does it to hold it against others who fall short, and to hold themselves up as better than the rest, while failing to maintain it themselves.

teachings.title: The Lord taketh pleasure in His people
teachings.summary: Against Eliphaz's claim that God doesn't care for righteousness, the Lord delights in His people's righteousness, and Eliphaz's accusations came from envy.
teachings.text:
Where Zophar the Naamathite kept his argument to generally true sayings, only hinting at Job's supposed guilt being the cause of his suffering, Eliphaz the Temanite, in his final outburst, lays charge to Job.

He accuses him of great wickedness and infinite iniquity. Breaking pledges, and the arms of the fatherless. Stripping the poor of their garments and refusing to feed them, or give water to the thirsty, bread for the hungry. Sent widows away empty handed. He even accuses Job of engaging in the level of wickedness mankind had reached before the flood.

It seems as though the railing accusations come from a resentment of Job's well-known perfection in his faith. The righteous living that made God point him out to Satan to begin with.

Eliphaz claims that God is not pleased by well doing, and doesn't care if man makes his ways perfect, complete and mature.

This seems like sour grapes.

We know that God not only doesn't delight in the destruction of the evil, that He would that all men be saved. The Lord takes pleasure in His children's righteousness.

**Psalm 149:4-5**
*For the Lord taketh pleasure in his people: he will beautify the meek with salvation. Let the saints be joyful in glory: let them sing aloud upon their beds.*

**Psalm 35:27**
*Let them shout for joy, and be glad, that favour my righteous cause: yea, let them say continually, Let the Lord be magnified, which hath pleasure in the prosperity of his servant.*

God does rejoice at men's repentance towards the truth, and our turning from sin to separate ourselves to His service.

When we do well for others, we let our light so shine that He is glorified among men.

Eliphaz is correct in one thing; the gospel.

*Receive, I pray thee, the law from his mouth, and lay up his words in thine heart. If thou return to the Almighty, thou shalt be built up, thou shalt put away iniquity far from thy tabernacles.*

That the humble before Him are delivered, and their needs met.

But he uses this truth as an accusation against Job, presuming he has taken pride in his own righteousness, and not humbled himself as Eliphaz clearly thinks he has.

He is a hypocrite, and I believe it stems from feelings of inadequacy and envy when he compares himself to Job. This also feeds his fears, that if it can happen to such a good man, how can Eliphaz avoid similar wrath in judgement?

And so, Job must be the worst.

teachings.title: The wise son and the diligent hand
teachings.summary: Proverbs contrasts the diligent, righteous and wise with the lazy fool; God provides for those who work, and the wise gather the harvest, including winning souls.
teachings.text:
**Proverbs 10** begins the more familiar listing of wise sayings, made in the Spirit by Solomon, his proverbs. But the lesson contrasting the righteous listening to instruction, being industrious, refraining from speaking evil and being wise, with the fool who is lazy, full of iniquity and violence, with a froward mouth, continues to be the primary theme carried over from the introduction in chapters 1-9.

Verse 1 contains an eternal truth that any parent could attest to. Establishing early the wisdom to found is accurate and true. A wise son is the pride of a dad, while the foolish son is the heaviness and sorrow of his mother.

From this base, the sayings stack up, precept upon precept, truth on truth. Building a foundation of wisdom that, sadly is lacking in the world today, because most, even many Christians, don't harken to the word of God. They do not fear Him, and so do not have His wisdom to rely on. They do not acknowledge Him in all their ways, and so He isn't there to direct their paths.

There are also proverbs given that have become ingrained in the secular lexicon (even if they don't acknowledge it). Such as the first half of verse 2; Gain made by wicked deeds profit nothing. In other words, crime doesn't pay. But the wise counter to this truth is that the way of the righteous delivers one from death.

We are told the truth of the Lord that He will provide for His own, the righteous won't famish, while He destroys the substance of the wicked. Not a prosperity gospel, but the understanding that when you walk in the Spirit, working in righteousness, the Lord will take care of your basic needs.

**Luke 12:27-31**
*Consider the lilies how they grow: they toil not, they spin not; and yet I say unto you, that Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. If then God so clothe the grass, which is to day in the field, and to morrow is cast into the oven; how much more will he clothe you, O ye of little faith? And seek not ye what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink, neither be ye of doubtful mind. For all these things do the nations of the world seek after: and your Father knoweth that ye have need of these things. But rather seek ye the kingdom of God; and all these things shall be added unto you.*

This is a promise of Christ Jesus Himself, with the caveat that the poor often are that way by being slackers, not diligent in their works.

**2 Thessalonians 3:10**
*For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.*

God blesses those that prepare, gathering in the summer against the winter is wise. Sleeping through the harvest is a shame. Being forward thinking and considering the end of something, understanding consequences, cause and effect, is wisdom. Shortsighted sin leads to shame.

Of course, the harvest analogy is not just applicable to agrarian cultures, or to earthly financial goals, but also the sharing of the gospel of Christ's Kingdom is frequently likened to the harvest.

**John 4:35**
*Say not ye, There are yet four months, and then cometh harvest? behold, I say unto you, Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest.*

Go soul-winning! The workers are few and the harvest is plenty. He that winneth souls is wise.

**Psalm 126:6**
*He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.*

But the sluggard who buries his talent of silver, to mix metaphors, he will be ashamed. He will not have sheaves of glory to rejoice in.

Being a just man, fair and merciful, extending grace to others, brings blessings and glory. The Lord will esteem the name of the just but the fool will die unknown, they will fall.

Walk upright, consider what you say. Don't be a prattling fool or a subtle and froward man, or a man of violence and offense, stirring up strifes and hatred. Knowing love covereth all sins.

**1 Peter 4:8**
*And above all things have fervent charity among yourselves: for charity shall cover the multitude of sins.*

teachings.title: The desires of the righteous granted
teachings.summary: God repeatedly promises to grant the desires of those who trust and walk in His way, so we should ask for heavenly treasure such as serving God and winning souls.
teachings.text:
Wisdom is for the lips of the man with understanding, the rod is for the back of those without it. The wise lay up knowledge against the future, keeping instruction, but the fool is always near destruction and refuses to be corrected.

The chapter is rich with promises for the righteous, including the desires of those walking the path of the Lord being granted, while the wicked do without and live in want and fear.

**Mark 11:24**
*Therefore I say unto you, What things soever ye desire, when ye pray, believe that ye receive them, and ye shall have them.*

**Psalm 37:4-5**
*Delight thyself also in the Lord: and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart. Commit thy way unto the Lord; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass.*

The consistent promise of God for those that trust in Him is repeatedly given throughout the Bible.

But seek the treasure in Heaven, not riches on this earth. Opportunity to serve God, to win souls, to help the poor and heartbroken. To judge the fatherless. Ask for this treasure and you will be blessed beyond measure.

The fear of the Lord prolongs your days. Brings knowledge and understanding. Provides for your needs and will grant you your desires.

 A wise man watches what He says, giving wisdom and speaking truth. The mouth of the wicked is perverse.

*The way of the Lord is strength to the upright: but destruction shall be to the workers of iniquity. The righteous shall never be removed: but the wicked shall not inhabit the earth*.

Amen

teachings.title: The scorner seeketh wisdom and findeth it not
teachings.summary: Those who hate God are given over and never find wisdom, so the wise keep silent under accusation as Christ did and flee foolish teachers rather than sifting knowledge from them.
teachings.text:
Continuing in **Proverbs 14**, we are given several wise sayings, often repeating the points to really drive them home. Archetypes of wisdom contrasted with the folly of fools and warnings against liars.

The wise builder, embodied especially in the "wise woman" of verse 1 who "*buildeth her house*," representing constructive, diligent wisdom that strengthens family, home, and community, where the foolish woman destroys her home, as plucking a hen. Bit by bit.

Again, we are told the upright fear the Lord. This healthy respect for God is the source and substance of wisdom. But those on the crooked ways of the perverse hat the Lord.

They have been made to know the truth, by the wrath of God revealed from Heaven against the ungodly, but they hate Him and truth.

**Romans 1:28**
*And even as they did not like to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not convenient*

God will give the wicked what they desire, and by rejecting them utterly, give them over to their perverse ways to their own destruction.

The fool speaks out because of pride, but the wise keeps their lips quiet when insulted. This is a hard one for many, including myself. Hard to remain quiet when being falsely accused and raised on or our pride is attacked. But Jesus showed us the way;

**Matthew 27:11-14** 
*And Jesus stood before the governor: and the governor asked him, saying, Art thou the King of the Jews? And Jesus said unto him, Thou sayest. And when he was accused of the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing. Then said Pilate unto him, Hearest thou not how many things they witness against thee? And he answered him to never a word; insomuch that the governor marvelled greatly.*

Humility in the face of accusations is often the most potent defense. Counterintuitive but like much of God's wisdom, it goes against man's understanding.

*Where no oxen are, the crib is clean: but much increase is by the strength of the ox.*

There are tradeoffs in life, and we are better for it. Sometimes, to get things done you have to be willing to shovel the dung. Another example of delaying gratification to your betterment.

Faithful witnesses do not lie, but a false witness will. It seems obvious, and repeated in verse 25: *A true witness delivereth souls: but a deceitful witness speaketh lies.* When given the opportunity, we should remember the deliverance we received, and speak truth to deliver others. This is pleasing to God and foundational in the 10 Commandments. Thou shall not bear false witness.

*A scorner seeketh wisdom and findeth it not...* reminds me of the false teacher, a reprobate who Paul describes in **2 Timothy 3:7** *Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.*

How can they, without the fear of God? How can they when they scoff at truth and hold it in unrighteousness? When they hate God rather than fear Him?

So we should reject the foolish man when you perceive he does not have knowledge. Again, flee a false prophet or someone claiming to know who just spouts nonsense. They ultimately will lie and speak falsehoods and defend their pride. They make a mock of sin, joking about evil ways. Flee these people. Don't take company with them, and don't try to sift any knowledge from them. They may be right about something, but in the end it isn't worth the rest that comes with it.

*The heart knoweth his own bitterness; and a stranger doth not intermeddle with his joy.*

No one but you and God can know the heartache or the joy you feel in your heart. Truly know it. And you can't know another's, even when you empathize or rejoice with them. It's an important thing to keep in mind when others deal with you, or you're dealing with others. Have grace because of this limitation, and thank God for it, too. If our heart were open to men, it could be embarrassing and shameful. Thank God we don't actually wear our hearts on our sleeve.

teachings.title: The fear of God divides wicked and righteous
teachings.summary: The wicked, without fear of God, flatter themselves in pride and love iniquity and end in hell, while those who fear God receive His mercy, protection and imputed righteousness.
teachings.text:
A short song ruminating on the wicked, **Psalm 36** turns this doctrine into prayer for the children of God, singing His praise.

The workers of iniquity come to a bitter end. They are cast down and fallen. Hell will be their home.

**Matthew 7:22–23**
*Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works? And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.*

They trust themselves, their "wonderful works," and with their lips they may claim the Lord, but their heart is far from Him.

Their pride comes as a snare. They do not fear God, and it is evidenced by the boldness of their sin. They lie to themselves, flattering their deeds to justify them in their own eyes until their sin is found hateful, that is, to be despised.

They lie to themselves, are haters of truth. They reject wisdom and well doing, and rather seek mischief and evil for others. They go out of their way to treat others spitefully, while not hating evil as we are commanded to.

**Romans 1:32**
*Who knowing the judgment of God, that they which commit such things are worthy of death, not only do the same, but have pleasure in them that do them.*

We are commanded to hate evil and cleave to what is good. They take pleasure in iniquity, even in seeing other wicked men committing it.

But for them that fear God, His mercy extends forever, His faithfulness spans the heavens. His righteousness stands like great mountains and His judgments as the great deep of oceans.

We sing praise to His lovingkindness and seek the protection of being under His wing. His provision for us is the *fatness of* His *house*, being in Christ makes us to drink if the living waters, the fountain of life, the river of His pleasure, constantly flowing to those who love God.

He is the true light, and in it we see Jesus.

**John 1:4–5**
*In him was life; and the life was the light of men. And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.*

The contrast between the wicked and righteous is the fear of the Lord. The love of truth and abhorring evil. The prideful versus the humility of falling before God, and seeking His lovingkindness and protection, and receiving His imputed righteousness upon the upright of heart. Amen

teachings.title: A soft answer and every idle word
teachings.summary: A soft answer and pure words please God, but every idle word will be judged at the Great White Throne, which should drive men to the salvation that spares believers that humiliation.
teachings.text:
**Proverbs 15** begins by again establishing the truth that things we say, and the manner we say it, is a key instruction for holy living.

A soft answer, given in kindness and grace can calm a situation. The tongue of the wise uses knowledge and disperses it.

A wholesome tongue, speaking pure words is a tree of life. Both spiritually, by the gospel, but also metaphorically by lifting up others' spirit. Plans and purposes rely on wise counsel, and many counselors make them established.

How we use our mouth, the words we choose, the knowledge we impart, the instruction we give, all is ultimately judged by God.

**Matthew 12:36**
*But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment*.

Because of this, the grievous words that engender strife, stir up anger, or the mouth that pours out foolishness, all is ultimately vanity, and the man who hasn't humbled himself to the Lord, and received justification through Christ will surely be ashamed at the judgment. Imagine every foolish or wicked thing you've ever said in anger, read aloud by the holy God for all to hear.

Every perverse word that causes others' spirit to fall. Every ignorant thing that led others astray. Every contention and strife stirred up by our unwise words, lack of discretion and wisdom, all revealed from the Great White Throne.

I thank God for His great salvation, that spares me from such utter humiliation. This alone should convict man to repentance towards the gospel.

We see that even the thoughts of the wicked are an abomination to God, but pure words are pleasing to Him. A soft answer and pure words, instruction and knowledge, these please the Lord, and they are good to our soul, and are a blessing to the people in our life.

*A man hath joy by the answer of his mouth: and a word spoken in due season, how good is it!*

How good it is to hear the joy of a brother when we are feeling down! The comfort in our mourning, being told exactly the thing we needed to hear, with all due wisdom and counsel, this is a gift to all, one we should spread ourselves.

teachings.title: Out of the abundance of the heart
teachings.summary: Our words are a window to our heart, and God, who sees hell and destruction, knows every thought and word.
teachings.text:
The words we say, the things that our tongue forms and passes our lips, is a window to our heart.

**Matthew 12:34**
*O generation of vipers, how can ye, being evil, speak good things? for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh*.

The heart of the fool prevents their lips from speaking wisdom. The heart one without understanding seeks foolishness to fill it, rather than understanding. The righteous' heart studies that they may give good answer to those seeking wisdom, but the wicked heart causes evil things to pour out the mouth of the fool.

Every thought and word is known by God.

*The eyes of the Lord are in every place, beholding the evil and the good.*

The Lord is omnipotent and omniscient, ever present and knowing all things. Not only the words we speak, but the heart we keep.

*Hell and destruction are before the Lord: how much more then the hearts of the children of men?*

If the dead and hell are tormented in the presence of the Lamb, before God night and day, how much more our hearts are known by Him?

**Psalm 44:21**
*Shall not God search this out? for he knoweth the secrets of the heart.*

The heart rejoices in the light of the eyes, a message of good report. Being the bearer of glad tidings, the reproof of life, the gospel...all this serves to brighten the heart of many, if they are inclined to wisdom and seek truth. Of course the fool rejects reproof and correction, to their shame.

teachings.title: Death and life in the power of the tongue
teachings.summary: Proverbs teaches that men are judged by their words, that offended brothers are hard to win, and that Jesus is the friend who sticks closer than a brother.
teachings.text:
Rounding out the chapter, we see multiple appeals to wisdom, more warnings of the tongue and its power, and eternal truths we can live by.

Our spirit can either get us through sickness and infirmity, or make us a burden to others.

Prudent men seek to gain knowledge. It's the mark of a wise man. The gift of wisdom can open doors and the gift of prudent speech, bring us before great men.

Offending a brother can cause contention that cannot be fixed. Family feuds can be near impossible to resolve. Better to avoid them, with soft words and prudent speech.

By the same token, Jesus says to forgive our brethren not just seven times in a day, but 70 times 7. Essentially, for every transgression. Humility and meekness and being a peacemaker is a blessing to others and God blesses us in return.

Again and again, Proverbs hammers home the power of what we say, what comes out of our mouth, the gift of an excellent spirit that say right things, by the fear of the Lord and the wisdom gained by walking in His ways, versus the death and misery of the foolish tongue.

*A man's belly shall be satisfied with the fruit of his mouth; and with the increase of his lips shall he be filled. Death and life are in the power of the tongue: and they that love it shall eat the fruit thereof.*

Ultimately, regardless of what we say, it will be what we are judged on. In this life or the next;

**Matthew 12:36**
*But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.*

I thank my Savior, Jesus Christ that I will not have all my thoughts of foolishness and froward speech repeated before God and all creation to my eternal shame, because of the gift of salvation in His blood. But in this life, we will be judged by our words and will have an accounting, so be prepared to by them. The fruit of what we say. So let your yea be year and your may be nay.

Finally, short sayings of sage advice; a man who finds a wife has found a good thing and the favor of the Lord. Amen to that. They are a helpmeet to the husband, and precious.

The poor will humbly ask, where the rich demands, so be prepared for this. We've already been taught that soft answers are wise, and a sign of humility. The rich's rough answer is a sign of pride and arrogance. Entitlement.

And lastly, *A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.*

This wisdom on friendship, and it's practical application is clear and often cited; to have friends you must be friendly yourself. More than pleasant and kind in your dealings, but loyal and true. Be a friend that sticks closer than a brother.

I think there is a spiritual application for this as well, and again, pointing to the gospel;

**John 15:13**
*Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends*

Jesus loves us, He died for us, in our place. And by being made sons of God, He is closer than any brother.

**Hebrews 2:11-12**
*For both he that sanctifieth and they who are sanctified are all of one: for which cause he is not ashamed to call them brethren, Saying, I will declare thy name unto my brethren, in the midst of the church will I sing praise unto thee.*

What love is this, that Jesus has for His sheep? What a gift that love from a friend closer than a brother. Rejoice in Him. Amen

teachings.title: Talebearers, evil surmising and discord
teachings.summary: Lying for sport, talebearing and evil surmising kindle strife and sow discord among brethren, one of the things God hates, and such haters will fall into their own pit.
teachings.text:
Next, we see that it is like a mad man randomly firing arrows, flaming arrows and sowing death to be a neighbor who lies to his neighbor for sport. To be "funny." To rile up a reaction through lies.

The spirit behind it is the same. Seeking mischief to stir up strife is wicked as Hell.

Finally, vs 20-22 and vs 23-28 deal with stirring up strife by being a talebearer and a liar. Strife caused by that little member, the tongue, that has such great power.

**James 3:5-6**
*Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth! And the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity: so is the tongue among our members, that it defileth the whole body, and setteth on fire the course of nature; and it is set on fire of hell.*

Talebearing and spreading rumors acts as kindling, as coals, keeping a fire going or sparking new fires.

Gossiping to stir contention, to bring about trouble where there is none, causing wounds of the heart, is *like a potsherd covered with silver dross.* A shard of a broken pot, with the impurities and refined waste of silver. Worthless and wicked.

Haters will lie and build up deceit within them. Paul warns Timothy of this kind of man;

**1 Timothy 6:4-5**
*He is proud, knowing nothing, but doting about questions and strifes of words, whereof cometh envy, strife, railings, evil surmisings, Perverse disputings of men of corrupt minds, and destitute of the truth, supposing that gain is godliness: from such withdraw thyself.*

Evil surmising is the act of harboring unproven, malicious suspicions, assuming the worst motives about others without evidence. It is a destructive, divisive attitude that often produces pride, strife, and envy. They take innocent actions of someone and inventing malicious intent, spreading rumors to others to poison them against the hater's target of ire.

Someone filled with hate can typically be characterized as having an unhealthy obsession with accusations that ruin fellowship, and sow discord among the brethren. Vs 25 specifically links discord and the other 6 things God hates, the 7 abominations from **Proverbs 6:16-19**, to these hate filled liars, flatterers, and talebearing deceivers;

*These six things doth the Lord hate: yea, seven are an abomination unto him: A proud look, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood, An heart that deviseth wicked imaginations, feet that be swift in running to mischief, A false witness that speaketh lies, and he that soweth discord among brethren.*

Don't be one, obviously, but also don't fall victim to one by listening to their talebearing. Their evil will be exposed and shown the whole congregation. The pit they dig to trap others will trap them. The stone they roll to crush their targets will return unto them. Their lying tongue and flattering mouth works ruin.

teachings.title: The fool uttereth all his mind
teachings.summary: Proverbs 29 teaches restraint of speech, that all men share one end so we should seek the eternal in Christ, and that children raised without the rod and fear of the Lord multiply the wicked as foretold for the last days.
teachings.text:
Continuing in **Proverbs 29:11**

*A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards*.

Keeping your tongue, holding back your opinions and thoughts, is a measure of wisdom. Discerned speech, as we have seen repeated in Proverbs, is valuable. Blabbing every idle thought that comes into your head is vain.

Rulers who believe lies, he will be surrounded by wicked servants. This could have dual meaning. Either, due to his own delusion and desire to be told lies, only the wicked prosper in his court. Or, if he is acting on lies, the servants carrying out his will are made wicked. Both are true.

Vs 13 is another reminder that we all, rich or poor, good or wicked, are given life by the same Lord. Another way of expressing the opposite end of life found in **Ecclesiastes**;

**Ecclesiastes 2:14**
*The wise man's eyes are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness: and I myself perceived also that one event happeneth to them all.* 

**Ecclesiastes 9:2**
*All things come alike to all: there is one event to the righteous, and to the wicked; to the good and to the clean, and to the unclean; to him that sacrificeth, and to him that sacrificeth not: as is the good, so is the sinner; and he that sweareth, as he that feareth an oath.*

If all men are alive, their eyes lightened by the Lord, and all men die, having the same end, then all the things we gather, the vows we make, the wood, hay and stubble we accumulate, all is vanity. We should have no respect of persons and we should all seek that which is eternal, in Christ. This is the way.

*The king that faithfully judgeth the poor, his throne shall be established for ever.*

There is truth in the saying, that a good king or ruler will judge the poor fairly and righteously, and prosper. But only one King has faithfully judged all men, who are all poor in His sight, and His throne is established forever. Christ Jesus.

Vs 15 is another admonition to not spare the rod of correction for a child. Feral children, left to their own foolishness, undisciplined, will bring their mother to shame.

Vs 17 is a companion to 15, *Correct thy son, and he shall give thee rest; yea, he shall give delight unto thy soul.*

Sandwiched in between these sayings, vs 16 says; *When the wicked are multiplied, transgression increaseth: but the righteous shall see their fall.*

The fastest way of multiplying the wicked is to raise a generation without fear of their parents or fear for the Lord. They lack wisdom, fear of the Lord is its foundation. They shame their parents. They indulge themselves and think not of others. The city is made bloody and lacks defenses against the stranger.

But vs 16 also is prophetic.

**2 Timothy 3:1-7**
*This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come. For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy, Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good, Traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God; Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away. For of this sort are they which creep into houses, and lead captive silly women laden with sins, led away with divers lusts, Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.*

The wicked will be multiplied, but the righteous shall see their fall. In the end times, we who have overcome in Christ will see the wrath of God poured out on them.

Where there is no vision, no righteousness of a king that follows the law, where there is no understanding of the ways of the Lord, the promises of God though His commandments, no prophecy and appreciation for the end times promise and eternal rewards, the people will perish.

teachings.title: I will keep my mouth with a bridle
teachings.summary: Like David and James we bridle the tongue, sometimes keeping silent rather than speak in anger, and remember man's life is a handbreadth compared to the glory to come.
teachings.text:
David writes that he made it a point of emphasis, that he would not sin with his mouth, to take heed of what he said. Keeping his tongue as with a bridle on a mule or a horse.

James, the brother of Christ, writes of the importance of this in his epistle.

**James 3:2–10**
*For in many things we offend all. If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man, and able also to bridle the whole body. Behold, we put bits in the horses’ mouths, that they may obey us; and we turn about their whole body. Behold also the ships, which though they be so great, and are driven of fierce winds, yet are they turned about with a very small helm, whithersoever the governor listeth. Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth! And the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity: so is the tongue among our members, that it defileth the whole body, and setteth on fire the course of nature; and it is set on fire of hell. For every kind of beasts, and of birds, and of serpents, and of things in the sea, is tamed, and hath been tamed of mankind: But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison. Therewith bless we God, even the Father; and therewith curse we men, which are made after the similitude of God. Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be.*

And it ought not be. But as David goes on to say, it can be difficult. He set out to do what was right, keeping silent even when it may have done good to speak, careful in his speech to not say the wrong thing, and in his silence, his sorrow was stirred.

Mature Christians, especially parents with adult children, or pastors with a flock, should recognize this feeling. When we see others doing evil, or worse, people we love being led away towards it, and we know if we speak out, correct them, especially in anger, that we'd do more harm than good.

The situation where we aren't angry with the person, but we know what the Bible says. Where we gently suggest and correct, but withhold our own opinion because we know it will lead us to sin, and give the others cause to justify their own evil. Where we will do more harm than good.

*My heart was hot within me, while I was musing the fire burned*.

But David's first instinct is to open his mouth to the Lord, and in his sorrow and burning heart, he asks *make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is: that I may know how frail I am*. Asking, how much longer to I have to suffer this?

Answering his own question, he notes the short lifespan of man, the handbreadth of years, especially compared to the eternal God. *Verily every man at his best state is altogether vanity.*

In the end, we know our life here is brief, and the pain we endure is nothing, especially compared to the glory to come and the eternity with the Lord.

**Romans 8:18**
*For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.*

This perspective, the finite life vs everlasting, can be a comfort. But it also can be a sobering reminder. That when taken together, men's lives are vain. People experience needless worry, anxiety, and inner turmoil over fleeting things like the accumulations of wealth.

Life is brutal and short. Our own tongue betrays us. Those we see around us constantly striving for temporary gain, often at the expense of their spiritual good, only to die, taking nothing of it with them into eternity.

*And now, Lord, what wait I for? my hope is in thee.*

For those of us with Heaven as our home, who knows that being absent from the body is to be present with the Lord, the futility of this world can be a sorrowful burden at times.

And the knowledge that the things that vex us, that the silence we take up is not only to keep us from sin, but recognizing that our complaints may well stem from how much we deserve what we get.

teachings.title: The strange woman and the wife of thy youth
teachings.summary: The strange woman of Proverbs 5 is both folly and literal adultery, which Solomon himself fell into, and the cure is to rejoice in the wife of thy youth and keep to God's straight path.
teachings.text:
**Proverbs 5** continues the introduction section of the book of wisdom, and the near pleading of the father, Solomon, to his son, but in the Spirit, God the Father pleading with His children, to pay attention and listen to what He is teaching us.

His instruction on chasing Wisdom, as knowledge and discretion, and warning of chasing after the strange woman of folly.

But Solomon being the pen used by the Penman, the analogy given in this chapter of adultery serves as both a metaphor and practical application of chasing after women who aren't yours. Something the king with a thousand wives and concubines knows all about.

So we can apply both literal and figurative and receive wisdom from both.

The strange woman speaks sweet sayings, and is seductive in her ways, but her end is bitter and sharp. Deadly.

God's paths are straight and knowable, a path of life, but her ways are moveable, ultimately unknowable. The Way is laid out and the light of that path is His word. The path of death shifts and moves and is full of snares and stumbling stones. Where you could think you know where you are and what lies ahead, and suddenly you're turned around and lost.

In an adulterous relationship, this is also true. What may start in lust and be seen as temporary, often leads somewhere else, and far away.

As they say: Sin will take you further than you want to go, keep you longer than you want to stay, and cost you more than you want to pay.

Don't go looking for the strange woman. Don't seek out the folly of other men's understanding. It can cost you your honor, and take away years of your life to the service of the cruel, your wealth and labors to the stranger.

Again, literally in the case of chasing after strange women, foreign women. Unsaved women. Women who are not your wife.

In **1 Kings 11** we read, *king Solomon loved many strange women...he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines: and his wives turned away his heart. For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods: and his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God, as was the heart of David his father.*

The wisest man in history, who wrote these warnings to his sons and to us, fell prey to the very thing he counseled against.

Solomon may have written this in repentance and regret. He may have been in the midst of it. It could be before he succumbed to the temptation. But it is often true that the preacher preaches what he needs to hear, more than the audience.

Verse 11 ties the literal back to the spiritual, and death and hell that awaits those who didn't fear God and seek after His Wisdom. The regret the fool will have as his flesh and body are consumed in never ending torment.

*How have I hated instruction, and my heart despised reproof; And have not obeyed the voice of my teachers, nor inclined mine ear to them that instructed me!*

The shame in the midst of the assembly of being almost in all evil, when the books are opened in judgment...If physical death from a lifetime of bad choices and sin is heartbreaking, the regret in Hell for those that didn't harken to the gospel must be overwhelming.

Solomon then compares fidelity to the wife of your youth, your first love, as with Lady Wisdom, to a fountain, to a well. To the cistern you dug. The waters are yours and you need not look for another source.

*Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.*

Don't stray from your wife. Don't stray from the instruction of your fathers. Be ravished always with her love. Be satisfied in her.

Our sins are before the Lord, He knows all our ways. A man's iniquities are the bonds he is caught in, the cords he is held with. Going after folly and rejecting instruction leads to a man's own sin binding him unto death.

teachings.title: The harlot's snare and the goodman gone
teachings.summary: The harlot's seduction of the simple young man is both literal and a picture of sin, whose lie is that the goodman, Christ, is far off and judgment delayed.
teachings.text:
Again, Solomon appeals to his son to take heed to wisdom, to bind it in his heart. To keep the commandments he's given him that he may live. The law as the apple of his eye. Making wisdom and understanding your sister and kinswoman that they keep you from the strange woman, which is death.

To illustrate, he gives a parable of a young man, void of understanding, who encounters a woman dressed as a harlot, who subtly entices him to bed.

He says such a woman is loud and stubborn and exists on every corner, just as folly and temptations are around every bend in the way.

She catches him, kisses him and saying she's holy, having made her offerings and confirming her vows, she beguiles him. Sheep's clothing for a ravenous wolf.

She appeals with flattery, she sought him special, seeking to find only him, while she is a snare to any who cross her path.

She appeals with the lust of the flesh. With enticing sensual carnality. Perfumed bed, preciously adorned to spend the night in passion. To take the fire to his  bosom. To spark that desire in his heart.

She says the Goodman of the house is not home, and gone for a long journey...making it illicit and adultery. There likely is no "goodman" as a harlot keeps no husband. But there is an allegory here for sin and the temptation that judgment of God is afar off. The Goodman which is Christ, not here.

Similar to the warning of complacency Jesus gives us;

**Matthew 24:44-51**
*Therefore be ye also ready: for in such an hour as ye think not the Son of man cometh. Who then is a faithful and wise servant, whom his lord hath made ruler over his household, to give them meat in due season? Blessed is that servant, whom his lord when he cometh shall find so doing. Verily I say unto you, That he shall make him ruler over all his goods. But and if that evil servant shall say in his heart, My lord delayeth his coming; And shall begin to smite his fellowservants, and to eat and drink with the drunken; The lord of that servant shall come in a day when he looketh not for him, and in an hour that he is not aware of, And shall cut him asunder, and appoint him his portion with the hypocrites: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.*

There is an allure to this idea, that we may justify sin by the distance of judgment. By the illusion of safety given by distance and time. But all who are fooled by this are found out.

And so; *With her much fair speech she caused him to yield, with the flattering of her lips she forced him.*

Temptations often come through flattery and fair speech, the things we make rationalizations with, like weaving a net for a snare.

And the fool falls headlong into it. Until they get trapped. The dart in the liver. The knife taking their life. Like a bird in a net.

This parable, taken literally, has played out innumerable times. We may all know simple young men who have fallen for it. But allegorically, it is true of folly, of rejecting wisdom for sin. For rejecting God's path of life to go our own way.

*For she hath cast down many wounded: yea, many strong men have been slain by her. Her house is the way to hell, going down to the chambers of death.*

teachings.title: Stolen waters are sweet
teachings.summary: Folly, the strange woman, lures both the simple and the wise through covetousness, and sin lieth at the door, but her guests are in the depths of hell.
teachings.text:
In contrast to the feast of wisdom and the prudence of going forth to invite all, the strange woman sits at the door of her house, and calls to those who cross her path.

She calls to the simple, that so often turn in to her. And, to the wise, she tempts them. Rather than with the sumptuous feast of wisdom, she offers the lure of covetousness. Of the appeal to the evil of the heart. Stolen waters are sweet, and secret bread pleasant. The heart that desires that which isn't theirs can guide even the wise to folly and sin.

As the Lord said to Cain*, if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door.* Sin becomes a master unto you.

Those that enter in to folly, to sin, wise and fools, enter into death, for her guests are in the depths of Hell.

teachings.title: Give not thy strength unto women
teachings.summary: Lemuel's mother warned against giving strength to women, the very thing that brought strife and blood on David's house and turned Solomon's heart.
teachings.text:
The final chapter of **Proverbs**, attributed to the mother of King Lemuel, which is considered a pseudonym or pet name for King Solomon (meaning "devoted to God"), and possibly what Bathsheba called her son. This wisdom is a mother's, and as impactful as any given by a father. As we know, we should not forsake the law, or instruction of our parents.

**Proverbs 1:8-9**
*My son, hear the instruction of thy father, and forsake not the law of thy mother: For they shall be an ornament of grace unto thy head, and chains about thy neck*.

And so here, we are privy to some of the sayings given a king by his mother. It begins with the loving devotion a mother has for her son, born of her womb, the fruit of her vows. A special relationship that fathers are blessed to witness and to share with their own mother, unique in the bond shared.

Regardless of her identity, or his, we have the Spirit inspired wisdom given to us.

*Give not thy strength unto women, nor thy ways to that which destroyeth kings*.

Women and being given to many wives were not just problems Solomon carried, but they were a downfall for his father David, as well.

King David had eight named wives and an unspecified number of additional wives and concubines taken after he moved from Hebron to Jerusalem.

Mical, his first, King Saul's daughter, who became bitter against him and had no children by him.

Maacah, daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur, mother of Absalom, the son who rebelled against David, and of their daughter, Tamar.

Ahinoam, the Jezreelitess, mother of Amnon, whose rape of his half-sister Tamar led Absalom to be bitter against David.

During the rebellion of Absalom, he "*went in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel*" on the roof of the palace, using them to humiliate David, and to make his claim to the throne through them.

David's lust for Bathsheba, which led to the murder of Uriah the Hittite, her husband, the death of David's first son with her, as punishment from the Lord.

All these things, and more, made David a bloody man, whose life was filled with strife and death. Thus, despite his desire to build the temple of God in Jerusalem, he was told he would not be allowed to;

**1 Chronicles 22:8**
*But the word of the Lord came to me, saying, Thou hast shed blood abundantly, and hast made great wars: thou shalt not build an house unto my name, because thou hast shed much blood upon the earth in my sight.*

Bathsheba, having been witness to all these things, may well have imparted this wisdom of experience to her Lemuel. To her second son and living heir of David, in hopes that he would not foresake the law of his mother, and suffer the same as her husband.

But in the end, we all fall short of the glory of God. Solomon was given the blessing of God to build the temple, which David had provisioned for. But his heart was not always right with God, for he gave his strength to women, and his ways to that which destroyeth kings.

teachings.title: The greatest commandment and the scribe near the kingdom
teachings.summary: Jesus summed the law in loving God and neighbour, both quoted from the Old Testament, and the scribe who humbly sought scripture was near the kingdom.
teachings.text:
This scribe is getting it. He knows the scriptures and sees that Jesus has answered all that the Pharisees and Sadducees have come at Him with, as the scribe likely knows the scriptures better than they do, given his station.

And he asks what is a defining question of Christ, to give the greatest commandment of God. And Jesus Christ the Son of God, the word, sums up the whole of the law on two points:
*Love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength: this is the first commandment. And the second is like, namely this, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.*

Some say here Jesus has invented new doctrine, because they not knowing the scriptures don't know that Jesus has simply quoted the first of the 10 commandments from Exodus and that loving thy neighbor as yourself comes from Leviticus.

On these two points rests the whole of the Law.

(Some like to point at love thy neighbor' as new doctrine, to say Jesus was more liberal and hippy-dippy than the God of the OT, but Leviticus 19:18 where this is found, is located in the same teachings that deal with stoning sodomites and adulterers)

The scribe agrees with Jesus answer, and adds to it from scripture prompting Jesus to say how near the Kingdom he is. Both physically, being in the presence of Christ, and spiritually, being so close to the truth, having faith from the word.

The contrast between this scribe and the Pharisees and Sadducees, is the difference between earnestly seeking the knowledge of God from his word and thinking themselves wise becoming fools.

Many such cases.

People with a predetermined idea of what they want God's word to say cannot be swayed from their belief in themselves. From their own reasoning. But those who earnestly seek wisdom, and humbly allow God's word to reveal it to them gain understanding. It's just how it works.

*For the LORD giveth wisdom: out of his mouth cometh knowledge and understanding. He layeth up sound wisdom for the righteous: he is a buckler to them that walk uprightly. He keepeth the paths of judgment, and preserveth the way of his saints*

teachings.title: Ye cannot serve God and Mammon
teachings.summary: There is no prosperity gospel; part of the cost of discipleship is giving of our wealth without fear or greed, laying up treasure in Heaven.
teachings.text:
This is a theme Jesus has been hammering home; the cost of discipleship.

Jesus said we must be willing to hate our family for His sake, and willing to give up our lives. To love others more than ourselves. To not worry for earthly things like food, shelter, raiment. To be willing to forsake all in service to others, that the Gospel be shared.

And, to use what wealth we have in that same service to Christ. *Lay not up ye treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal: for where your treasure is, there will your heart be.*

Of all the warnings of the costs of true discipleship, of truly following Christ, this one against Mammon, love of money, not only giving up trying to be rich and gaining stuff, but giving away the stuff you already have, is the hardest for most people to face.

There is no "prosperity gospel." God provides what we need and knows our needs even when we don't. We may even be blessed with wealth but it's not our own. We are supposed to give all, and yet most of us don't even want to give a 10% tithe to our own church.

This can be greed, and it often is. Jealously guarding our treasure here. That it's where our heart is, not Heaven.

But for many, it's fear. Fear of doing without. Fear that God won't take care of us. That if we give away that which is extra in our lives that others benefit and by our works, God be glorified, we will suffer need. This fear grips especially tight in times like this where the debt economy, inflation and taxation and other worldly pressures weigh heavily upon us.

We may not be called to forsake everything we own. But we are called to at least consider it and do it where appropriate, in the measure called for. To be hospitable. Charitable. To do unto others without thought of ourselves and our own comfort.

In two more chapters we will see the rich young man sit down with Jesus and say in all things he is righteous before the law, and Jesus will say ok, sell everything you have and give it all away to follow Me. And the rich young man will walk away. He was being shown the error of his thinking that he was righteous by his works, and most of us won't be called to forsake all. God knows our limitations and infirmities. But we are called to give. To be as wise as this worldly unsaved steward. To not serve Mammon while claiming to serve God.

teachings.title: Divisions and pride in Corinth
teachings.summary: Paul rebukes the divisions in Corinth, for God uses the weak and foolish so that no flesh glories and the church is of one mind in Christ.
teachings.text:
Continuing the study of Spiritual Gifts, I want to refer to 1 Corinthians 12, which has the clearest writing on the topic, but first to establish the context of the epistle. Note Paul is writing at the request of a sister in Christ who reports that the church in Corinth has some troubles. Pride has set some brethren against others in respect to multiple issues.

The first being the source of their salvation, making it about the minister of the Gospel they received the word from, using the who as a way to puff themselves up. Paul and Apollos and Cephas camps, claiming a purer lineage in Christ. Of course Paul destroys this idea quickly. It isn't the minister, who sowed or watered or harvested, but the Lord who gains the increase.

And, as Paul says that his wish is the church at Corinth be of one mind in Christ, not filled with such divisions, because a church being united in the body of Christ is able to do great things for the Lord. But it can't if pride is giving way to error. Seeking our own glory, not glorying in the Lord.

Paul reminds them that God uses the weak, the seemingly foolish, to confound the wise and being to naught things that are, so that no flesh can glory in His presence.

Basically, to be humble and stop thinking you are a special boy. That not many wise men after the flesh, mighty men, nobles, are called. The wisdom of this world is not the wisdom of God.

And so it is in that spirit that Paul reminds them that they are there only in Christ, who God has made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption.

teachings.title: Cease ye from man
teachings.summary: Proud men who trust in men, riches and idols will hide in the rocks from the wrath of the Lamb, while the meek inherit the earth.
teachings.text:
**Isaiah 2** continues the clear teaching of the Lord, and the futility of those who trust in men, things of men like riches and chariots, and especially idols made with hands.

We know in Christ's wrath, on that great and terrible day, that the proud and haughty men will be brought low, and attempt to hide from His wrath:

**Revelation 6:15-17**
*And the kings of the earth, and the great men, and the rich men, and the chief captains, and the mighty men, and every bondman, and every free man, hid themselves in the dens and in the rocks of the mountains; And said to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him that sitteth on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb: For the great day of his wrath is come; and who shall be able to stand?*

They will be brought low and flee to the mountains and the caves and their bunkers and pray for the rocks to cover them, and there will be nowhere left to hide.

But the meek shall inherit the earth. The humble and poor of spirit are blessed by God through Christ.

And all nations will be under the King of kings. And be taught by Him, and walk in His paths.

Knowing this, Isaiah appeals to Judah, the house of Jacob. Why trust they in men? In the power of other nations to save them? In idols of gods made by hands? *Cease ye from man, whose breath is in his nostrils: for wherein is he to be accounted of?*

*O house of Jacob, come ye, and let us walk in the light of the Lord.*

Disobedient Judah, having the oracles of God, knowing the redemption of Christ to come, and the day of judgment to follow, and yet still they trusted in vanity. As so many do today.

teachings.title: Wisdom crieth, and God will laugh at their calamity
teachings.summary: Wisdom calls men to repentance as God did through the prophets and Christ, but those who hate knowledge are given over, and God will not answer but laugh when their calamity comes.
teachings.text:
Continuing **Proverbs 1**, we see a warning against joining in another man's sin. Not being led to robbery and violence by greed. That ultimately, it ends in their own blood and death. Crime doesn't pay.

Next, Solomon tells us of Wisdom, as a woman, though this is more the feminine of the word than a gendered being, and Wisdom is much like the Spirit of God, today.

The original Hebrew word for wisdom, *hokhmah*, is a feminine noun, and Solomon will compare the virtuous woman of Wisdom to the harlot, the "strange woman," the folly of fools later in the book.

But the literary device aside, like the male Spirit of God, He reproves and reproaches, and calls men to truth. Like God has done through the inspired word of the prophets, crying out, how long, ye simple ones? Scorners and fools reproofed.

Wisdom is "poured out" in spirit. Calling us to repentance. God's words, the wisdom itself, made known unto us. As God promises to write the law in our inward parts.

This echos so many passages, especially when Jesus rebukes the Jews;

**Matthew 23:37** *O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!*

**Isaiah 65:2** *I have spread out my hands all the day unto a rebellious people, which walketh in a way that was not good, after their own thoughts*

Those thoughts are foolishness. They set at naught His counsel. This crooked generation refused to accept His Wisdom, and so, He will laugh at their calamity. He will mock the. When their fear cometh.

What a sobering thing to be mocked of the Lord. To get to the place where you've been given up and given over. When you are destroyed in His presence, cast into eternal torment, and God will laugh, because He gave you ample warning. The wrath of God being revealed from Heaven, that you had no excuse. But they didn't wish to retain God in their knowledge.

*Then shall they call upon me, but I will not answer; they shall seek me early, but they shall not find me: For that they hated knowledge, and did not choose the fear of the Lord*

But those who fear the Lord, and receive wisdom from Him, have a better promise;

*But whoso hearkeneth unto me shall dwell safely, and shall be quiet from fear of evil*

teachings.title: Every word out of His mouth
teachings.summary: Since wisdom proceeds from the mouth of God and man lives by every word of God, we need a Bible that keeps every word, which in English is only the King James Bible.
teachings.text:
**Proverbs 2** continues the instruction on Wisdom, and The importance of accepting her as the truth of God. That Spirit of truth that we as Christians are given, so long as we receive it, walking in the Spirit, walking in God's word.

We go to church to hear the word preached (faith cometh by hearing), as we incline our ear unto wisdom. Not being, as many are described in scripture, dull of hearing. We should rather be ready to hear and to keep it in our hearts, as doers of the word.

We should seek the wisdom of God as it were silver, a treasure. More valuable than riches is the wisdom of God's commandments.

**Matthew 7:24** *Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock*

A wise man cries for knowledge, and lifts up their voice for understanding. Asking God for His wisdom, like Solomon did. Ask and it shall be given you. Seek it and ye shall find. And with knowledge, understanding, and in doing what God says, we grow in faith.

**Hebrews 11:6** *But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.*

*The Lord giveth wisdom.* Out of His mouth:

**Matthew 4:4** *But he answered and said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.*

If wisdom proceeds out of the mouth of God, and we live by every word of God, and all scripture is given, inspired by God, written by holy men of God who spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost, we need to have a Bible that conveys all of them. That we may be perfect, complete and throughly furnished having everything we need. In English, this is found only in the authorized version of the King James Bible, the perfect and preserved word of God.

teachings.title: Get wisdom: a father's urgent instruction
teachings.summary: As David urgently taught Solomon to get wisdom, every parent's priority should be to impart the fear and knowledge of God and keep children from those who cause them to stumble.
teachings.text:
Solomon continues giving the reader what is essentially a preface for the Book of Proverbs, that runs through chapter 9. The understanding of Wisdom vs folly, the good woman to be sought vs the strange woman, who leads to ruin.

While there are plenty of wise sayings given in the first 9 chapters, including here in **Proverbs 4**, the thrust of Solomon's instruction is to emphasize this choice, and to encourage the pursuit of God's will, His paths, knowledge, discernment and Wisdom.

He recalls his father David's instruction, stressing this idea.

*Keep my commandments, and live. Get wisdom, get understanding: forget it not; neither decline from the words of my mouth. Forsake her not, and she shall preserve thee: love her, and she shall keep thee. Wisdom is the principal thing*...

She brings honor, promoting the wise, and more importantly, leads to a crown of glory through the ornament of grace.

The pursuit of Godly wisdom is inextricably linked to accepting the truth of God in His gospel. The fear of God is the beginning of wisdom, but the end of it is grace and glory.

Note the urgency of David in instructing his son, reflecting in Solomon's own words to his sons, and by the Spirit, to we who are sons of God.

This should be every parent's priority, too.  Imparting this same understanding, that in wisdom is life, and that if you prioritize knowledge of God, you will not stumble, He will direct your paths, you have life in Him.

Coupled with the warning to not follow after the wicked, the froward, the evil. Those who are only satisfied by mischief and by causing others to stumble. Taking pleasure in harming others. In violence. In offense.

This is literally true, referring in previous chapters to those who rush to spoil and bloodshed. But it is also true of those who, rather than instruct children to go down the paths of Wisdom, instead mislead and bring children to offense.

**Luke 17:2** *It were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and he cast into the sea, than that he should offend one of these little ones.*

And so, like David to Solomon, the king urges his children to not let these sayings depart from them. To keep them. To not turn to the left or the right. To keep our heart with all diligence. To ponder the path of our feet. In all our ways acknowledging God, that He may direct us where to go. To keep on the Way. To remove our foot from evil.

teachings.title: Wisdom's feast and the gospel invitation
teachings.summary: Wisdom's feast pictures the gospel invitation in which Christ the bread of life calls all, simple and wise, good and bad, to come and freely take the water of life.
teachings.text:
**Proverbs 9** concludes the preface of Proverbs, the instruction of Solomon to his son on Lady Wisdom and the strange woman of folly.

Wisdom's table is set for the feast, her house ready, her wine mingled (the restoration of the preserved fruit of the vine mixed with water, spiced with myrrh, sweetened with honey), her maids sent to call all who would enter in to come.

*Whoso is simple, let him turn in hither: as for him that wanteth understanding, she saith to him, Come, eat of my bread, and drink of the wine which I have mingled.*

The unadulterated truth of God's word is that wine. The bread which has come down from heaven is Jesus.

**John 6:32-36**
*Then Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Moses gave you not that bread from heaven; but my Father giveth you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is he which cometh down from heaven, and giveth life unto the world. Then said they unto him, Lord, evermore give us this bread. And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst. But I said unto you, That ye also have seen me, and believe not.*

Her maidens calling out to the feast of Wisdom as the parable of the wedding feast:

**Luke 14:16-23**
*Then said he unto him, A certain man made a great supper, and bade many: and sent his servant at supper time to say to them that were bidden, Come; for all things are now ready. And they all with one consent began to make excuse. The first said unto him, I have bought a piece of ground, and I must needs go and see it: I pray thee have me excused. And another said, I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to prove them: I pray thee have me excused. And another said, I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come. So that servant came, and shewed his lord these things. Then the master of the house being angry said to his servant, Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in hither the poor, and the maimed, and the halt, and the blind. And the servant said, Lord, it is done as thou hast commanded, and yet there is room. And the lord said unto the servant, Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled*.

Just as both the simple and the wise are compelled to turn hither to Wisdom's feast, so too the gospel is for both good and bad;

So those servants went out into the highways, and gathered together all as many as they found, both bad and good: and the wedding was furnished with guests.

**Matthew 22:10**
*So those servants went out into the highways, and gathered together all as many as they found, both bad and good: and the wedding was furnished with guests.*

Jesus crying out in the streets, telling all to come to Him;

**John 7:37-38**
*In the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink. He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.*

Forsake the foolish and live! Whosoever will, let him come.

**Revelation 22:17**
*And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely*.

The invitation of God to wisdom, to knowledge and understanding, is the invitation to life; as a wedding feast laid out by the host. Where the wise enters into the meal already prepared. The wine mingled. The wedding clothes, laid out, white and pure. To eat that bread of life and drink that living water, never to hunger or thirst again.

teachings.title: Be not envious against evil men
teachings.summary: Solomon's later proverbs read like Paul's epistles in teaching believers not to envy or keep company with evil men nor partake of their sins, showing the single unified wisdom of God throughout the Bible.
teachings.text:
Deep in the meat of the word, the heart of these sayings, we really can capture the themes that have been being hammered, again and again, and see the Gospel of hope that is in Proverbs.

To me, these later sections seem almost to be a New Testament epistle, and much of it would fit there.

The Epistles of Paul highlight the implications of salvation on the Christian life. Solomon's wisdom does much the same thing.

**2 Corinthians 6:14**
*Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?*

Be not envious of evil men, or desire to be with them. Don't take part in another man's sin.

**1 Timothy 5:22**
*Lay hands suddenly on no man, neither be partaker of other men's sins: keep thyself pure.*

**1 Corinthians 5:11**
*But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat.*

**Ephesians 5** is full of such wisdom;

*Let no man deceive you with vain words: for because of these things cometh the wrath of God upon the children of disobedience.Be not ye therefore partakers with them*...

*And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them.*..

*See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time, because the days are evil. Wherefore be ye not unwise, but understanding what the will of the Lord is. And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit*...

*Nevertheless let every one of you in particular so love his wife even as himself; and the wife see that she reverence her husband.*

The wisdom of God is clear and consistent throughout the Bible. We are given parable, story, sayings that all convey a single, unified message. The way of God. His ways are not our ways, yet we may know Him, because He has shown us in His word. What a blessing.

teachings.title: Jesus dumb before His accusers, appointed to destruction
teachings.summary: Christ, silent before Pilate and Herod, fulfilled Isaiah 53 and Lemuel's charge to open the mouth for the dumb, leaving the rulers of Judea without excuse.
teachings.text:
**Vs 8-9** *Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction. Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy.*

The call to be a voice for the condemned without a voice, for the poor and needy, is the way of Kings and pleasing to God.

Jesus, appearing before the judgment spoke not at all.

**Matthew 27:12-14**
*And when he was accused of the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing. Then said Pilate unto him, Hearest thou not how many things they witness against thee? And he answered him to never a word; insomuch that the governor marvelled greatly.*

Jesus, appointed for destruction and mute to give His cause, directly exemplifies this saying. While Pilate could be excused for not knowing the proverbs (or the prophecy;
**Isaiah 53:7** *He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth.*) Herod, King of the Jews, and the presits and scribes should have.

**Luke 23:8-9**
*And when Herod saw Jesus, he was exceeding glad: for he was desirous to see him of a long season, because he had heard many things of him; and he hoped to have seen some miracle done by him. Then he questioned with him in many words; but he answered him nothing.*

A fit ruler should speak for the condemned, to ensure justice. To consider the judgment. To plead the cause of those brought before them by the powerful, to ensure the poor and powerless aren't being falsely accused.

The knowledge given to Lemuel by his mother was certainly heard by those princes of Judea, by their King, and ignored. What should have convicted them in the heart, witnessing Jesus, silent before them, instead was an indictment, that they had no excuse.

teachings.title: The snare of the strange woman and Eve's deception
teachings.summary: Solomon's finding of few upright men and no upright woman, with 1 Timothy 2, acknowledges woman's nature to be deceived while she can still be the virtuous woman, equal in Christ and subject to her husband.
teachings.text:
Finishing up on **Ecclesiastes 7**, the Preacher explains that, even as he proved his argument from wisdom, and sought understanding, there are still things he fails to know.

He has seen the vanity and folly of life, the endless cycles where there is a time for every purpose under Heaven. That there is nothing new under the Sun. That man's labors are endless, the travails of life grinding, that death comes for us all. He has learned that God blesses man to enjoy what we have, but that seeking much increase leads to more trouble. Not necessarily more blessings.

He has found that the lazy, unjust and wicked receive His wrath in due time, but even the just man may come to an early end, while the wicked continues on. That the lessons learned in mourning, the inevitable death of all men, are more valuable than the mirth and enjoyment of our labors.

He has sought wisdom and been given understanding from God that all have sinned and fallen short of His glory. That even as we judge the fool and the iniquity of others, waiting for their recompense and fall, we have our own account of sin. That judgement comes for us all.

*All this have I proved by wisdom: I said, I will be wise; but it was far from me.*

The wisest man to ever live still falls short of the depth and riches of the Lord.

**Romans 11:33-36**
*O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! For who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor? Or who hath first given to him, and it shall be recompensed unto him again? For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen.*

Solomon applied his heart to know and search and seek wisdom, to know the reason of things. The wickedness of folly, foolishness and madness. He considered all things under the Sun and burdened himself with much knowledge.

And from it all, even the understanding of death and the bitter end we all face, he could not comprehend the ways of women.

We all know Solomon's weakness was the women he married, the concubines he kept. That by going after their strange gods to please them, he brought curses upon his kingdom.

He says, in his experience, that women have a heart full of snares and nets. The allegory in Proverbs of the strange woman of folly, who takes in the young and simple, bringing  them to their death echoes his words here. But more, he says that while only one in a thousand men he has found to be upright, he has yet to find an upright woman.

We know by **Proverbs 31** that such a virtuous woman may exist, but is rarer than rubies.

Solomon sees that those that please God may escape from the snare of the woman, the strange woman, but the sinner is taken by her. As Adam was by Eve.

**1 Timothy 2:8-14** 
*I will therefore that men pray every where, lifting up holy hands, without wrath and doubting. In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array; But (which becometh women professing godliness) with good works. Let the woman learn in silence with all subjection. But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence. For Adam was first formed, then Eve. And Adam was not deceived, but the woman being deceived was in the transgression.*

The view of women as more mercurial and prone to follow their volatile emotions, doesn't discount their ability to *continue in faith and charity and holiness with sobriety.* To strive to be that virtuous woman. To be as lady wisdom. To be blessed with children. To be equal in Christ while subject to her husband. It is just acknowledging the nature of the female, as much as the nature of man to sin.

*Lo, this only have I found, that God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions.*

As rare as a good man, made upright by God, may be, the inventions of evil in a man's heart are still our nature.
